title: Uttanka's grudge
hookLine: a student loses a queen's earrings to a disguised snake king, and carries his anger all the way to Janamejaya
carry: krodha: anger is an enemy within
tomorrow: can one snakebite make every snake guilty?

cards: A student finishes his studies and asks his teacher what fee he can pay.
The teacher sends him to ask his wife, and she names it: the earrings worn by the queen of King Paushya, brought back in time for a rite she means to wear them to. The student is Uttanka.
The queen gives him the earrings, with a warning: Takshaka, the king of the snakes, wants them badly. Be careful. On the road home, Uttanka sets the earrings down to wash before his prayers.
When he looks up, they're gone.

teach.b: The beggar was Takshaka in disguise. He slips into a hole in the earth, down into the world of the snakes, and Uttanka follows.
Down there it's like a dream: two women weaving with black and white threads, a wheel turned by boys, a man with a horse.

teach.h: SMOKE AND FIRE; THE EARRINGS BACK.
teach.b: The man tells him to blow into the horse; smoke and fire pour through the snake world, and a frightened Takshaka hands the earrings back.
Uttanka pays his teacher in time. Done, you'd think. But he can't let it go.
He travels to King Janamejaya and says: Takshaka killed your father. Avenge him. So the snake fire doesn't start with the king's grief alone.
It starts with a student's grudge, carried a long way and set beside someone else's wound. Hindu teachers have a name for what's moving here.
Anger, krodha, is one of the six enemies within, the shadripu: desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride and envy. Not enemies out there; enemies in here.

And in the Bhagavad Gita, which sits inside this very epic, Krishna traces how anger travels: dwelling on something breeds attachment, attachment breeds desire, blocked desire turns to anger, anger clouds the mind, and a clouded mind forgets what it knew.
Uttanka was a good student. He'd won. But he kept dwelling, and his anger found a king with a bigger wound.
Anger spreads like that, not always from the one who was hurt, but from the one beside them, saying: don't let this go. Next, a snake speaks up for mercy.

how: Paying a teacher's fee at the end of study, guru dakshina, is a custom some Hindu students still keep, often as a gift or a service the teacher asks for. In the Adi Parva, Uttanka's journey ends at Janamejaya's court, and that is where the snake sacrifice begins to be urged.

o: a book of rules for what a student owes his teacher
the closing book, where the snakes make peace with the king
the opening book, where a student's grudge reaches a grieving king

games.q: Uttanka and the earrings — tap the pairs.
p: stole them, disguised as a beggar

s: Takshaka stole the earrings in his snake form
he came as a wandering beggar and dropped the disguise as Uttanka chased him.
Uttanka urged Janamejaya to avenge his father
he told the king that Takshaka had killed his father.
the shadripu, the six enemies, are demons the gods fight
they're inside: desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride and envy. anger, krodha, is one.

games.q: your uncle keeps telling your dad he should still be furious at a cousin over an old money fight. by today's teaching, what fits?
o: anger is an enemy within; feeding it clouds judgment, whoever does the feeding.
family loyalty means your dad should stay angry.
it's fine to keep the anger as long as he never acts on it.
games.why: Uttanka's grudge, fed and carried, helped light a king's fire. Krishna's chain in the Gita runs from dwelling to anger to a clouded mind.

practice: Bring to mind a grudge you were handed rather than one that began with you: a family feud, a friend's complaint, an old story about a whole group of people.

Set it down in front of you, the way Uttanka set the earrings on the ground, and ask: whose was it first? Then notice where you are on Krishna's chain, dwelling, wanting, angry, clouded. Just see it, and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Adi Parva. The opening book, where a student's grudge reaches a grieving king's ear.

carryVoice: Keep this: krodha, anger, is an enemy within. Tomorrow: can one snakebite make every snake guilty? See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Paushya Parva (Uttanka and the earrings; his appeal to Janamejaya)
